subject: physics
question_text: Why does a heap of sand poured on the ground form a cone or pyramid shape?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 9 Very Short Answer Question 13 (printed p.99). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: dry sand grains are held only by inter-grain friction, so a heap can carry only a limited shear stress before the grains slide, and the slope of a stable heap therefore always settles at the angle of repose, giving the same cone/pyramid shape at any size. BOOK DISCREPANCY (book p.99): the printed answer gives the reason as "the lower layers are subjected to higher stress because of the weight above; the stress increases linearly with depth, leading to a pyramid shape". That is true of stress in ANY heap of any shape and is not the reason for the SHAPE. The shear-stress limit and the angle of repose, written here, are the actual reason a heap always settles into a cone or pyramid.

steps.why: A heap is built of loose grains, so the only thing holding a slope in place is friction between grains, and friction can supply only a limited shearing stress before the layers slide past each other.
common_mistakes: Giving only "stress increases with depth" as the reason for the shape. That happens in a heap of any shape and does not by itself explain why the heap is a cone or pyramid.
Saying the grains are bonded together. Dry sand grains are held only by friction, with no bonding force between them.
steps.memory_tip: Loose grains held only by friction can take just so much shear before they slide.
steps.margin_note: Marked for naming friction between grains and a limited shear stress — not for the stress-with-depth statement alone.

steps.why: Because every grain added to the pile slides until the local slope returns to the angle of repose, a stable heap keeps the same slope angle whatever its size, so it grows as a cone or pyramid rather than any other shape.
common_mistakes: Naming the angle of repose without saying it is the slope at which sliding stops. The angle itself is not the reason; reaching it is.
Describing the heap as pyramid-shaped only because of the weight above, which is the book's stress-with-depth reasoning and not the actual cause of the shape.
steps.memory_tip: Sand always slides back to the same angle, so every heap ends up the same shape.
steps.margin_note: Marked for naming the angle of repose as the slope where sliding stops, giving the heap a fixed shape.

insider_note: Naming only 'stress increases with depth' earns zero for the second mark — the examiner is checking for the shear-stress limit and the angle of repose, the actual reason for the shape.
